blocks: Playback — stored MIDI goes out to a hardware synth, or is turned into audio by an instrument such as Operator, ideally as an exact reproduction.
A DAW handles MIDI in three situations, each with an ideal:
Playthrough — MIDI from hardware passes through the DAW in real time to a synth or plug-in, ideally feeling as immediate as a piano.

Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:

Latency — a constant delay. Audio has to be buffered on its way in and out of an interface. Players adapt to small delays as long as they stay the same; even a piano has some delay between key and string.
Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:

Jitter — a random, varying delay. MIDI, audio and the interface run as separate processes with separate clocks, and moving events between them depends on the operating system and drivers. Jitter, far more than latency, makes timing feel loose.
Two problems keep computer MIDI from the ideal:

Ableton works from two assumptions: latency is better than jitter, because it is predictable, and when playing through while recording you want to record what you hear, even if that is slightly later than what you played.
Recording — the MIDI interface driver timestamps each event on arrival, and Live places the event in the clip by that timestamp.

Playthrough — Live delays events by a constant amount rather than playing them whenever the busy system gets to them. With monitoring on, it adds a delay based on the audio buffer size, so notes land in the clip where you heard them.
Playback to hardware — Live sends timestamps for the driver to schedule outgoing events. Windows MME drivers cannot use timestamps, so Live schedules those events itself.
During audio dropouts Live still receives and records MIDI correctly, even if playthrough sounds wrong; playback is accurate once the system recovers.
Timestamps only exist inside the computer. External hardware acts on MIDI as soon as it arrives.
MIDI cables are serial, so a chord's notes travel one after another; dense passages can smear timing.
Older synths may scan their own keyboards slowly, adding jitter. Problems multiply as more devices join the chain.
